fixes.explanation: Right, friend. Moses says, "You must not bring the wages of a prostitute, whether female or male, into the house of the LORD your God to fulfill any vow…" (Deuteronomy 23:18). Those wages stay out. The verse gives the reason: "…both are detestable to the LORD your God."

Yes, baker. Moses says, "You may charge a foreigner interest, but not your brother…" (Deuteronomy 23:20). The line is drawn between a brother and a foreigner. He ties it to a blessing on everything they put their hand to in the land.

Yes, friend. Moses says, "…you may eat your fill of grapes…" (Deuteronomy 23:24). That's generous. You walk in and eat until you've had enough. But hold that thought, because the basket comes up in the very same verse.

Right, friend. Moses says you "…must not put any in your basket." (Deuteronomy 23:24). You can eat your fill, but the basket stays empty. One verse gives both rules, and the basket is the one that says no.

Treasure isn't in the verse, friend. Moses says they "…did not meet you with food and water on your way out of Egypt…" (Deuteronomy 23:4). Gold and silver never come up. The text names food and water, and that's the answer.

Achan, a man of Judah, took what he shouldn't have at Jericho (Joshua 7:1). That's his story, and it isn't the one in this verse. Here Moses says they hired "…Balaam son of Beor from Pethor in Aram-naharaim to curse you." (Deuteronomy 23:4). Easy names to shuffle, friend.

Korah, a Levite, stood up against Moses in the wilderness (Numbers 16:1-3). This verse doesn't name him. The man it names is Balaam. Moses says they hired "…Balaam son of Beor from Pethor in Aram-naharaim to curse you." (Deuteronomy 23:4).

That's the twist! Moses says, "…the LORD your God turned the curse into a blessing for you…" (Deuteronomy 23:5). Balaam was hired to curse Israel. What the verse says came out for Israel was a blessing. Curse in, blessing out, baker.
Yes, baker. The verse gives the reason itself: "…because the LORD your God loves you." (Deuteronomy 23:5). That is the reason the text gives. Short and sweet, and it's plenty.

That's it, friend. Moses says, "The third generation of children born to them may enter the assembly of the LORD." (Deuteronomy 23:8). He's talking about Edomites and Egyptians. Just before it, he says an Edomite is a brother and that Israel lived as a foreigner in Egypt (Deuteronomy 23:7).

The tenth generation shows up earlier in the passage, but it belongs to the Ammonites and Moabites. For them it's a no: they may not enter even to the tenth generation (Deuteronomy 23:3). For Edomites and Egyptians, Moses says, "The third generation of children born to them may enter the assembly of the LORD." (Deuteronomy 23:8). Third, friend, not tenth.

Settling arguments isn't in the verse, friend. Moses says the LORD "…walks throughout your camp to protect you and deliver your enemies to you." (Deuteronomy 23:14). Protecting and delivering is the job described. Nothing about tents or arguments.

Yes, friend. Moses says, "Let him live among you wherever he chooses, in the town of his pleasing." (Deuteronomy 23:16). The choice is his. Right before that, Moses says not to return a slave to his master if he has taken refuge with you (Deuteronomy 23:15).

A widow? Nothing in these verses about widows, baker. Moses says, "You may charge a foreigner interest, but not your brother…" (Deuteronomy 23:20). The line he draws is brother versus foreigner. The whole verse turns on that line, so keep your eye on it.

Judge is a heavy word, friend, and it isn't the one here. Moses says, "…so that the LORD your God may bless you in everything to which you put your hand in the land that you are entering to possess." (Deuteronomy 23:20). The aim is blessing. And it reaches everything they put their hand to.

Not quite, baker. Moses says you may eat your fill of grapes, but you "…must not put any in your basket." (Deuteronomy 23:24). The basket is where the line is. Eating in the vineyard is fine, and putting grapes in the basket is not.

That's it, baker. Moses says you may pluck the heads of grain with your hand, but "…you must not put a sickle to your neighbor’s grain." (Deuteronomy 23:25). Hand is allowed. Sickle is the line. One word, big difference.

No fire in this verse, baker. Moses says, "…you must not put a sickle to your neighbor’s grain." (Deuteronomy 23:25). The sickle is the tool named, and the hand is what's allowed. A torch never shows up.
